name: Olanzapine/Fluoxetine (Symbyax)
summary: Once-daily combination capsule used for bipolar I depression and treatment-resistant depression. Can be very effective, but comes with real baggage: weight gain/metabolic risk, sedation, and a boxed warning about suicidality in younger people.
description: Symbyax combines olanzapine (an atypical antipsychotic) with fluoxetine (an SSRI). It’s used for bipolar I depression and for depression that hasn’t responded to multiple antidepressant trials. It’s taken once nightly and can help mood and sleep, but it commonly causes weight gain and metabolic changes (blood sugar, cholesterol, triglycerides). It also carries antidepressant boxed warnings about suicidal thoughts/behaviors in children, teens, and young adults, plus an antipsychotic boxed warning about increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.
patient_summary: Symbyax is a nightly capsule that combines an antipsychotic (olanzapine) with an SSRI (fluoxetine). It’s used for bipolar I depression and for treatment-resistant depression. It can help when other meds haven’t, but it often causes weight gain and metabolic changes, and it has serious boxed warnings—especially about suicidality risk in younger people and higher mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis.

linked_conditions.context: Labeled for acute depressive episodes associated with bipolar I disorder. Taken once daily in the evening; dose is adjusted based on response and tolerability.
Labeled for treatment-resistant depression (typically defined clinically as nonresponse to at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials in the current episode).

contraindications: Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) intended to treat psychiatric disorders (concurrently, within 5 weeks of discontinuing olanzapine/fluoxetine, or within 2 weeks of discontinuing the MAOI)
Initiation in a patient receiving IV methylene blue
Use with thioridazine (do not initiate thioridazine until 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine-containing therapy)

efficacy_response.metric: Clinical response in bipolar depression or treatment-resistant depression
efficacy_response.percentage_value: Varies by person and study design
efficacy_response.patient_text: Symbyax is one of those meds that can move the needle when standard antidepressants haven’t—especially in bipolar depression and treatment-resistant depression. The tradeoff is tolerability: weight gain, sedation, and metabolic changes are common and can become the reason people stop it.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral capsule; can be taken without regard to meals
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Long half-life effects due to fluoxetine and active metabolites; interactions may persist for prolonged periods after discontinuation
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Refer to individual components (fluoxetine and olanzapine); smoking may lower olanzapine levels; hepatic impairment can decrease clearance and increase exposure
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: May be taken without regard to meals

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Symbyax (olanzapine/fluoxetine) is a once-daily evening capsule used for two specific mood-depression targets: bipolar I depression and treatment-resistant depression. It’s not a general-purpose antidepressant, and it’s not a first-line pick for most people because the metabolic side effects can be intense.
items: {link:condition:bipolar-disorder:Bipolar I Disorder (acute depressive episodes)}: Depressive episodes in bipolar I (not mania)
{link:condition:treatment-resistant-depression:Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD)}: Depression that hasn’t responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials in the current episode

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Here’s how this med tends to feel in real life. Not everyone gets all of this, but these are the patterns people describe:

quotes: It didn’t flip a switch, but after a couple weeks I realized I wasn’t stuck in the pit as much.
My depression felt less sticky—like I could actually move through the day again.
It didn’t make me euphoric. It just made life feel possible.
I take it at night because it knocks me out.
It helped me sleep, but the next morning I felt heavy.
The calm was nice… the grogginess, not so much.
items.note: Night dosing is standard because olanzapine can be sedating.

quotes: The hunger was unreal. Like my body didn’t have an off switch.
I could feel the weight creeping up even when I wasn’t trying to overeat.
It worked for my mood, but the weight gain became the dealbreaker.
items.note: Weight gain and appetite increase are common and can be significant.

quotes: I got edgy and restless at first, like I couldn’t sit still.
It helped depression but I had to watch for hypomania signs.
My doctor warned me: if I start sleeping less and feeling 'too up,' call immediately.
items.note: Fluoxetine can trigger activation; antidepressants can precipitate mania/hypomania in vulnerable people—screening and monitoring matter.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Symbyax is taken once daily at night. Some people notice sleep/sedation changes early, but the depression benefit usually builds over time.
key_points: First doses: You may notice sedation, appetite changes, or restlessness before mood improves
First 1-2 months: This is the highest-monitoring window for suicidal thoughts/behavior changes and mood destabilization
Long tail after stopping: Fluoxetine has a long half-life, so effects and drug interactions can linger for weeks

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Symptom improvement in bipolar depression and treatment-resistant depression
sections.text: Symbyax is specifically positioned for people with bipolar I depression or depression that hasn’t responded to multiple antidepressants. In practice, it can be a strong option when standard SSRI/SNRI strategies aren’t enough—but tolerability (especially weight/metabolic effects and sedation) often decides whether someone can stay on it long-term.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warnings: suicidality risk (younger patients on antidepressants) and increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis (antipsychotics).
sections.black_box:
Suicidal thoughts and behaviors: Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. Monitor closely for clinical worsening and emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors, especially during the first 1 to 2 months of therapy and during dose changes. Olanzapine/fluoxetine is not approved for children younger than 10 years.

Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis: Antipsychotic drugs increase the risk of death in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Olanzapine/fluoxetine is not approved for the treatment of dementia-related psychosis.
other: Metabolic risk: weight gain, increased triglycerides and cholesterol, hyperglycemia—monitor labs and body weight
Sedation and CNS depression: can impair driving, reaction time, and judgment
Mania/hypomania risk: antidepressant component can precipitate mood elevation—screen for bipolar disorder and monitor
QT prolongation risk (fluoxetine): higher concern with risk factors, electrolyte issues, and other QT-prolonging meds
Serotonin syndrome risk when combined with other serotonergic agents
SIADH/hyponatremia risk (SSRIs), especially in older adults and those on diuretics
Blood dyscrasias: leukopenia/neutropenia/agranulocytosis reported with antipsychotics—monitor CBC when clinically indicated
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): rare but life-threatening antipsychotic reaction
DRESS and severe hypersensitivity reactions (olanzapine-associated): discontinue if suspected
Increased fall risk from somnolence and orthostasis
patient_counseling: If you’re under 25, take the suicidality warning seriously—tell someone you trust and keep close follow-up, especially early on and during dose changes.
Call your clinician immediately for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe agitation, panic, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania.
Expect appetite and weight changes to be possible. Don’t wait months to address it—early planning matters.
Avoid driving or high-risk tasks until you know how sedating it is for you.
Know the red flags for serotonin syndrome (confusion/agitation, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, fever) and NMS (fever, rigidity, confusion). These can be emergencies.
This medication is not for dementia-related psychosis in older adults.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: The big themes: sedation, appetite/weight gain, and metabolic changes (lipids, blood sugar). Some people also notice restlessness, tremor, and sexual side effects (from the SSRI component).
plain_language_list: Sleepiness / sedation (often why it’s taken at night)
Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision (anticholinergic-type effects from olanzapine)
Lab changes: higher cholesterol/triglycerides, higher blood sugar/A1C, prolactin changes, liver enzyme increases
Orthostatic dizziness (blood pressure drops when standing)

common.patient_note: This is one of the most common reasons people stop Symbyax. Hunger can feel louder, cravings can spike, and weight can move fast. Plan early: weigh-ins, waist measurement, nutrition strategy, and labs—don’t wait until it’s already a problem.
It can help sleep, but it can also make you feel slowed down. Night dosing helps. If mornings feel like wet cement, talk with your prescriber about dose adjustments or alternatives.

common.incidence: Triglycerides increased (adults: 16% to 51%); LDL/total cholesterol increases reported (ranges vary by age group)
common.patient_note: This med can raise triglycerides and cholesterol and can worsen blood sugar control. Labs aren’t optional—this is the 'check the numbers' medication.
Annoying but common. Sugar-free gum, hydration, and dental care matter because chronic dry mouth can wreck teeth.
Swelling (often ankles/legs) can happen. If it’s severe, painful, one-sided, or comes with shortness of breath, get evaluated urgently.
Stand up slowly. This is more likely in older adults and in people prone to low blood pressure. Falls risk is real.
Can feel like jittery hands or internal vibration. If it’s new, worsening, or comes with sweating/fever/confusion, think serotonin toxicity and get help.

serious: Suicidal thoughts/behaviors (especially in children, adolescents, and young adults early in treatment or during dose changes)
Mania/hypomania (mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, risky behavior)
Serotonin syndrome: agitation, confusion, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, fever, rigidity
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): fever, severe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability
Severe metabolic complications: marked hyperglycemia, ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar coma
QT prolongation and serious arrhythmias (higher risk with predisposition, electrolyte issues, or interacting drugs)
DRESS and severe hypersensitivity reactions (rash with systemic symptoms, eosinophilia, organ involvement)
Blood dyscrasias (neutropenia/agranulocytosis): infection risk, fever, sore throat

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Because this med includes fluoxetine (SSRI) and olanzapine (antipsychotic), interactions can be wide-ranging. The big ones are MAOIs, other serotonergic meds, QT-prolonging meds, and anything that increases sedation or orthostasis.

items.with: MAOIs (psychiatric MAOIs) and IV methylene blue
items.risk: Contraindicated due to high risk of serious toxicity, including serotonin syndrome.
items.action: Allow 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting olanzapine/fluoxetine. Allow 5 weeks between stopping olanzapine/fluoxetine and starting an MAOI.

items.risk: Contraindicated due to risk of serious cardiac arrhythmias/QT issues and drug interaction risk.
items.action: Avoid combination. Thioridazine should not be started until 5 weeks after discontinuing fluoxetine-containing therapy.

items.with: Other serotonergic agents (SNRIs, other SSRIs, triptans, TCAs, tramadol, fentanyl, methadone, lithium, buspirone, St. John’s wort, tryptophan, amphetamines)
items.action: Avoid risky combinations when possible. If used, educate on symptoms and monitor closely—especially during dose changes.

items.with: QT-prolonging meds or electrolyte problems (low potassium/magnesium)
items.risk: Higher risk of QT prolongation and dangerous arrhythmias.
items.action: Review med list carefully. Consider baseline and follow-up ECG in higher-risk patients and correct electrolytes.

items.with: Alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds
items.risk: Additive CNS depression → worse sedation, impaired coordination, higher fall risk.
items.action: Avoid or minimize sedatives. Counsel about driving and safety. If combined, use the lowest effective doses and monitor closely.

items.risk: Increased bleeding risk (SSRI effect on platelet aggregation).
items.action: Use caution and monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding symptoms—especially if combined with other bleeding-risk meds.

items.risk: Smoking may lower olanzapine levels, potentially reducing effect.
items.action: Tell your prescriber if you start/stop smoking—dose and response can change.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping Symbyax isn’t usually a cold-turkey situation. Even though fluoxetine has a long half-life (which can blunt classic SSRI withdrawal), both components can cause rebound symptoms if you stop abruptly—especially the olanzapine side (sleep, anxiety, agitation, and return of mood symptoms). Taper with your clinician unless there’s an emergency reason to stop.
key_points: Do not abruptly stop unless directed for a serious adverse reaction (e.g., serotonin syndrome, NMS, severe rash/DRESS).
Fluoxetine’s long half-life means some withdrawal symptoms can be delayed or less intense—but side effects and interactions can also linger.
Antipsychotic discontinuation can cause rebound insomnia, anxiety, agitation, GI symptoms, and return of mood symptoms; tapering reduces that risk.
If symptoms flare during taper (sleep collapses, agitation spikes, mood drops hard), slow the taper and reassess the plan.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Symbyax is typically taken once daily in the evening. Dosing is described in paired amounts: olanzapine (mg) + fluoxetine (mg). Your prescriber adjusts the dose based on response and tolerability. Safety of daily doses above olanzapine 18 mg and fluoxetine 75 mg has not been evaluated.

adult.bipolar_depression_initial: Olanzapine 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg PO once daily in the evening
adult.bipolar_depression_titration: Adjust based on response and tolerability; use caution with dose changes in patients prone to hypotension or with factors that slow metabolism (e.g., females, nonsmokers) or increased sensitivity to olanzapine
adult.bipolar_depression_usual: Olanzapine 6 to 12 mg / fluoxetine 25 to 50 mg PO once daily (evening)
adult.bipolar_depression_max: Safety of daily doses > olanzapine 18 mg / fluoxetine 75 mg has not been evaluated
adult.trd_initial: Olanzapine 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg PO once daily in the evening
adult.trd_titration: Adjust based on response and tolerability; consider lower starting doses (olanzapine 3 to 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg) in hepatic impairment, hypotension-prone patients, females, nonsmokers, or those sensitive to olanzapine
adult.trd_usual: Olanzapine 6 to 18 mg / fluoxetine 25 to 50 mg PO once daily (evening)
adult.trd_max: Safety of daily doses > olanzapine 18 mg / fluoxetine 75 mg has not been evaluated
adult.administration: Take once daily in the evening; may be taken without regard to meals

sections.simple_explanation: This combo is dosed as two medicines in one capsule: olanzapine (which can be sedating and increases appetite/weight risk) plus fluoxetine (an SSRI). It’s usually taken at night, and the dose is adjusted slowly to balance mood benefit with side effects—especially sedation and metabolic changes.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Symbyax can be used in select situations, but special populations require extra caution because the med affects metabolism, sedation, blood pressure, and metabolic labs.
sections.pregnancy: Olanzapine and fluoxetine cross the placenta. Refer to individual component guidance for risk/benefit decisions in pregnancy. Monitor closely if used, and involve psychiatry/OB when possible.
sections.lactation: Olanzapine and fluoxetine are present in breast milk. The manufacturer advises weighing infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and maternal treatment benefits. Refer to individual component guidance and monitor the infant if therapy is continued.
sections.pediatrics: Approved for acute depressive episodes associated with bipolar I disorder in children ≥10 years. Not approved for children <10 years. Pediatric patients have higher concern for metabolic syndrome risk with long-term olanzapine exposure; use caution and monitor metabolic parameters closely.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid for behavioral problems associated with dementia or delirium unless nonpharmacologic options failed and the patient is at risk of harming self or others. Boxed warning: increased mortality in dementia-related psychosis. If used for labeled indications (e.g., bipolar depression), consider starting lower (olanzapine 3 to 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg once daily in the evening) and adjust cautiously due to reduced metabolism and higher risks (falls, orthostasis, hyponatremia).
sections.hepatic: Start lower: olanzapine 3 to 6 mg / fluoxetine 25 mg PO once daily in the evening; adjust cautiously because metabolism may be decreased. Individual ingredient products may allow lower dose strengths if needed.
sections.smokers: Olanzapine levels may be lower in smokers; monitor response and adjust clinically as needed.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Suicidality and behavioral change: closely monitor for worsening depression, suicidal thoughts/behaviors, and activation symptoms (anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, mania), especially during the first 1-2 months and during dose adjustments
Weight/BMI: baseline; check at 8 and 12 weeks after initiation and dose changes; then at least quarterly (some clinicians check every visit)
Waist circumference: baseline and annually (especially if metabolic risk)
Fasting plasma glucose or A1C: baseline; ~4 months after initiation; then annually (more often if abnormal or high risk)
Lipid panel: baseline; ~4 months after initiation; then annually (more often if abnormal)
Vital signs including orthostatics: every visit (at least weekly in early weeks per higher-risk monitoring frameworks); reassess after dose changes
Sedation/alertness and fall risk: every visit, especially in older adults and during early treatment
CBC: as clinically indicated; monitor more closely in patients with low baseline WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia
Electrolytes/chemistries (including sodium): at least annually; check sodium as clinically indicated in at-risk populations (older adults, diuretics, prior hyponatremia/SIADH risk)
Liver function: periodically and as clinically indicated (olanzapine can increase transaminases; hepatic impairment increases exposure)
EPS and tardive dyskinesia: assess at every visit; formal rating scale at least annually (or every 6 months if high risk)
ECG: as clinically indicated in patients with QT-prolongation risk factors or concerning symptoms

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Symbyax is an oral capsule taken once daily in the evening. Generic equivalents are available in multiple fixed-dose combinations.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Symbyax combines two mechanisms. Olanzapine blocks several receptors involved in mood, dopamine signaling, and sedation—especially serotonin (5-HT2A/2C), dopamine (D1-4), histamine (H1), and alpha-1 receptors, with additional muscarinic effects. Fluoxetine boosts serotonin signaling by inhibiting serotonin reuptake. Together, the combo is thought to produce stronger antidepressant effects than either approach alone, likely through coordinated effects on serotonin and downstream dopamine/norepinephrine pathways.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Symbyax is a targeted tool, not a casual antidepressant. It’s typically considered when (1) someone has bipolar I depression and needs an evidence-based option that covers depression without using antidepressant monotherapy, or (2) someone has treatment-resistant depression and standard antidepressant strategies haven’t worked. The major limiting factor is metabolic and weight-related side effects—so the clinical conversation is usually: “Is the benefit worth the metabolic cost, and how are we going to monitor and protect you if we use it?”

seo.title: Olanzapine/Fluoxetine (Symbyax): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Warnings
seo.description: Symbyax (olanzapine/fluoxetine) for bipolar I depression and treatment-resistant depression: nightly dosing, major side effects (weight gain, metabolic changes, sedation), boxed warnings, interactions, and monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Symbyax (olanzapine/fluoxetine) is used for two things: (1) acute depressive episodes in bipolar I disorder, and (2) treatment-resistant depression—meaning depression that hasn’t responded to at least two adequate antidepressant trials in the current episode.
It’s taken once daily in the evening, and it can be taken with or without food. Night dosing is typical because olanzapine can be sedating.
It can. Many people feel more sedated at night, which can improve sleep. The flip side is that some people feel groggy the next day, especially at higher olanzapine doses.

faqs.q: What are the biggest side effects people notice?
faqs.a: The big three are: increased appetite/weight gain, metabolic changes (blood sugar and cholesterol/triglycerides), and sedation. Dry mouth, dizziness when standing, tremor, and restlessness can also happen.

faqs.q: Why does Symbyax have a suicidality boxed warning?
faqs.a: Because it includes an antidepressant (fluoxetine). Antidepressants have been shown in short-term studies to increase the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults. The key move is close monitoring early in treatment and during dose changes, plus involving family/caregivers when appropriate.

faqs.q: Is Symbyax safe for older adults with dementia?
faqs.a: No—Symbyax is not approved for dementia-related psychosis. Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning about increased mortality in older adults with dementia-related psychosis. This is a hard stop for most situations.

It can. Any antidepressant can push susceptible people into hypomania/mania. That’s why clinicians screen for bipolar disorder and monitor for reduced need for sleep, increased energy, racing thoughts, impulsivity, and risky behavior—especially early in treatment.

faqs.q: What medications should not be mixed with Symbyax?
faqs.a: MAOIs are a major no. You also generally avoid pimozide and thioridazine. And you have to be careful with other serotonergic meds (serotonin syndrome risk), QT-prolonging meds, and sedatives/alcohol because of additive impairment and fall risk.

faqs.q: How long do interactions last after stopping Symbyax?
faqs.a: Longer than many people expect. Fluoxetine has a long half-life, so effects and interactions can persist for weeks after discontinuation. This matters most when switching to MAOIs or other interacting meds.

faqs.q: Do I need lab monitoring on Symbyax?
faqs.a: Yes. This is a ‘check the numbers’ medication. Weight/BMI and metabolic labs (glucose/A1C and lipids) are standard, along with monitoring for sedation, orthostasis/falls, EPS/tardive dyskinesia, and sodium in higher-risk patients.

faqs.q: If Symbyax works, can I stay on it long-term?
faqs.a: Some people do, but the decision usually comes down to whether the benefits outweigh the metabolic cost. If weight or labs shift significantly, the plan may include lifestyle interventions, closer monitoring, dose adjustments, or switching medications.
